# Candidate sensor technologies
- Sensor-T2: thin-pitch sensor with large signal sharing.
- Sensor-T3: planar sensor, standard pitch.
- Sensor-T1: 3D-electrode sensor, larger pitch.
All are qualified for bump bonding to the readout chip.

# Irradiation and test-beam campaign, 2026
Sensors were irradiated with reactor neutrons to 2e16 neq/cm^2 and measured at the SPS test beam.
Hit efficiency after 2e16 neq/cm^2:
- Sensor-T2: 82.0% (strong charge trapping; full depletion no longer reachable at the maximum bias)
- Sensor-T3: 98.5%
- Sensor-T1: 99.2%
Requirement for the innermost layer: >= 97% up to end of life.

# Meeting notes 2026-03-02
Cooling: CO2 evaporative cooling at -35 C confirmed. Mechanics: the carbon-fibre staves are on schedule.

# Readout chip
The common readout chip supports 50x50 um^2 pixels and a 1.5 GHz/cm^2 hit rate. All candidates are compatible.

# Earlier simulation summary (2025, 150 um, unirradiated)
Single-hit resolution: Sensor-T2 6.0 um, Sensor-T3 9.0 um, Sensor-T1 14.0 um.

# Services
The power budget per module is 7 W. Serial powering is the baseline.

# Schedule
Sensor market survey closes in Q2; pre-production in Q4.

content.text:
I read all seven project documents and recorded the key facts. The documents contain no model of efficiency versus fluence or thickness, so the thickness question is still open.

- **Candidates:** Sensor-T1 is a 3D-electrode sensor with a larger pitch. Sensor-T2 has a thin pitch and large signal sharing. Sensor-T3 is a standard-pitch planar sensor. The documents give no per-technology thickness ranges, only the overall 50–300 µm limit.
- **Efficiency after 2e16 neq/cm² (2026 test beam):** T2 reached 82.0%, which fails the 97% requirement. The cause is strong charge trapping, and the sensor can no longer be fully depleted at maximum bias. T3 reached 98.5% and T1 reached 99.2%, so both pass. The document does not say what thickness these were measured at.
- **Unirradiated resolution at 150 µm (2025 simulation):** T2 gave 6.0 µm, T3 gave 9.0 µm and T1 gave 14.0 µm.
- **Other facts:** The readout chip supports 50×50 µm² pixels and a 1.5 GHz/cm² hit rate, and all three candidates are compatible. Cooling is CO2 at −35 °C and the power budget is 7 W per module. The documents give no bias voltage or threshold values.

T2 is excluded on efficiency. T3 is the likely choice, because it has the better resolution of the two sensors that pass. That depends on how efficiency changes with thickness, which I couldn't determine from the documents. The next step is to simulate T3 and T1 across thickness.

content.text:
The feasible set is empty, because none of the documents give enough evidence to confirm that any technology and thickness meets 97% at 2e16 neq/cm². I recorded this with `record_results`.

- **T2:** Excluded at every thickness. It measured 82.0% after 2e16 neq/cm², and the document attributes this to strong charge trapping and no full depletion at maximum bias. No thickness-specific data suggests it could pass.
- **T3 and T1:** Uncertain at every thickness from 50 to 300 µm. The 2026 test-beam document gives 98.5% for T3 and 99.2% for T1, which clear 97% by 1.5 and 2.2 points. It doesn't say what thickness was measured.
- **Missing data:** The documents contain no efficiency-versus-thickness model, trapping parameters, bias limits or threshold values. The simulation tool covers only unirradiated sensors, so it can't fill this gap.
- **Thickness caveat:** Thinner sensors give less signal against the threshold. Thicker sensors suffer more trapping and are harder to deplete. I did not assume the test-beam thickness was 150 µm, which is only the thickness of the 2025 simulation.

In the final recommendation, T3 gives the better resolution of the two non-excluded technologies, so it is the likely pick. The recommendation should be flagged as conditional on the unknown test-beam thickness.

| Thickness (µm) | T3 resolution (µm) | T1 resolution (µm) |
|---|---|---|
| 50 | 9.931 | 16.317 |
| 100 | 9.275 | 14.789 |
| 150 | 9.211 | 13.481 |
| 200 | 9.130 | 14.695 |
| 300 | 12.430 | 18.786 |

- **T3 vs T1:** T3 has the better resolution at every thickness.
- **T3 vs thickness:** T3 is nearly flat from 100 to 200 µm, at about 9.1–9.3 µm. It is worse at 50 µm and much worse at 300 µm. The roughly 1% differences within 100–200 µm are probably not significant.
- **T1 vs thickness:** T1 is best at 150 µm (13.5 µm) and worse at the other thicknesses.
- **Efficiency:** I still don't know how efficiency depends on thickness, because the test-beam thickness isn't stated. Within 100–200 µm, the thickness choice should therefore weigh efficiency risk. Thinner sensors give less signal and thicker ones suffer more trapping.

content.text:
**Recommendation: Sensor-T3 (planar) at about 150 µm, with a caveat.** The 97% efficiency requirement is not confirmed at that thickness.

- **T2 is excluded.** It has the best resolution, at 6 µm and 150 µm. But it reached only 82% efficiency after 2e16 neq/cm², well below the hard 97% requirement. The cause is strong charge trapping, and the sensor can't be fully depleted.
- **T3 beats T1 at every thickness.** T3's best unirradiated resolution is about 9.1–9.3 µm, and T1's best is 13.5 µm at 150 µm. The gap is about 4 µm, so the choice doesn't depend on how close the runner-up is.
- **Thickness matters little for T3 between 100 and 200 µm.** Resolution there is 9.275, 9.211 and 9.130 µm, a spread of about 1% that is probably noise. T3 is worse at 50 µm (9.93 µm) and much worse at 300 µm (12.43 µm).
- **Why 150 µm.** It sits in the middle of the T3 plateau. That balances the lower signal of thinner sensors against the extra trapping of thicker ones. It is also the thickness of the 2025 reference simulation. 200 µm is nominally best by 0.08 µm, which isn't significant, and it carries more trapping risk.
- **The efficiency evidence is uncertain.** The test-beam efficiencies (T3 98.5%, T1 99.2%) don't state the thickness they were measured at. The documents have no model of efficiency versus thickness. T3's margin over 97% is only 1.5 points.
- **Fallback.** If efficiency at the chosen thickness looks marginal, T1 at 150 µm is the safer option. It has a 2.2-point margin but a resolution of 13.5 µm.
- **Resolutions are unirradiated.** Radiation damage will degrade them.

content.text:
## Final recommendation: Sensor-T3 (planar), 150 µm

The 97% efficiency requirement at 2e16 neq/cm² is not confirmed at 150 µm, because the efficiency evidence doesn't state a thickness.

**Resolution.** The simulated unirradiated single-hit resolution is 9.211 µm. The 2025 reference at the same thickness was 9.0 µm.

**Efficiency evidence.**
- The 2026 test-beam document reports 98.5% for T3 after 2e16 neq/cm², which is 1.5 points above the 97% requirement.
- This comes from a document, not from simulation. The simulator only covers unirradiated sensors.
- The document doesn't state the thickness at which the 98.5% was measured. The documents also contain no model of efficiency versus thickness.

**Rejected alternatives.**
- **T2:** It has the best resolution (6 µm at 150 µm). It reached only 82% efficiency after 2e16 neq/cm², which fails the hard requirement. The document attributes this to strong charge trapping and no full depletion at maximum bias.
- **T1:** It passes at 99.2%, but its best resolution is 13.5 µm at 150 µm. T3 is about 4 µm better at 150 µm and better at every thickness I simulated. T1 at 150 µm is the fallback if T3's efficiency proves marginal.
- **Other T3 thicknesses:**
  - At 50 µm T3 gives 9.93 µm, and at 300 µm it gives 12.43 µm.
  - At 100, 150 and 200 µm it gives 9.275, 9.211 and 9.130 µm. That spread is about 1% and probably noise.
  - I chose 150 µm as the middle of that range, to balance the lower signal of thinner sensors against the extra trapping of thicker ones.

**Caveats.**
- The resolution is unirradiated and will degrade after irradiation.
- The documents give no bias voltage or threshold values.
- I recommend checking T3 efficiency at 150 µm with a test beam or irradiated simulation before finalizing.

T2 has the best resolution (6 um) but measured only 82% efficiency at 2e16 neq/cm2, so it fails the hard 97% requirement. Of the two technologies that pass, T3 resolves better than T1 at every simulated thickness. Its best resolution is about 9.1-9.3 um, against 13.5 um for T1. T3 is flat within about 1% over 100-200 um, so I chose 150 um, the middle of that plateau. This balances lower signal at smaller thickness against more trapping at larger thickness. The caveat is that the test-beam efficiency (T3 98.5%, 1.5 pt margin) has no stated thickness, and the documents have no efficiency-vs-thickness model. So 97% at exactly 150 um is not confirmed. The resolutions are unirradiated and will degrade after irradiation. T1 at 150 um is the fallback if T3's efficiency proves marginal. I recommend verifying T3 efficiency at 150 um.
